title: Prostate Cancer on the Internet-Information or Misinformation?
screen_reason: Structured review of the top 75 Webcrawler results for 'prostate cancer'; 39 sites carried prostate cancer information and were rated element by element. Alongside the quality components (currency, disclosure, attribution, interactivity, coverage), each information element was rated on a separate accuracy scale (1 mostly incorrect, 2 mostly correct, 3 completely correct) against a 50-element tool derived from Campbell's Urology, and the paper reports a share of items judged incorrect with a denominator: of 943 elements covered on 39 sites, 1% was 'mostly incorrect'. That is an explicit truth/falsity judgement against an external ground truth, so it is CONTENT rather than a quality score.

estimates.country: Not stated; websites retrieved by an unrestricted English-language web search, authors based in the United States, and the highest-coverage sites include non-US ones (e.g. the Australian Lions Society)
estimates.platform: Websites returned by the Webcrawler search engine for the term 'prostate cancer' (top 75 of 390,770 results)
estimates.date: Not stated (article submitted 11 June 2005, published May 2006)
estimates.measure_type: % of prostate cancer information elements on the reviewed websites rated 'mostly incorrect'
estimates.value_raw: Of 943 elements covered on 39 sites, 94% were completely correct, 5% were mostly correct and 1% was mostly incorrect.
estimates.denominator: 943 information elements actually covered across the 39 prostate cancer websites (from a 50-element rating tool applied to each site; only elements present on a site entered the denominator)
estimates.definition: The element received an accuracy rating of 1, defined in Table 1 as 'mostly incorrect', when judged against the content of the corresponding element in the rating tool derived from Campbell's Urology, 7th edition
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition of misinformation; accuracy was operationalised by the rating scale 'Accuracy: 1 Mostly incorrect, 2 Mostly correct, 3 Completely correct'
estimates.source_quote: Of 943 elements covered on 39 sites, 94% were completely correct, 5% were mostly correct and 1% was mostly incorrect.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, Results (p. 1836); the same sentence is repeated in the Discussion, p. 1838
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Rated by the research team (two urologists) against a purpose-built 50-element tool whose content was derived from the corresponding chapters of Campbell's Urology, 7th edition (1998), reproduced in Appendix 3. No inter-rater reliability statistic, no independent double coding, and no adjudication procedure is reported; the authors state that the main limitation is 'the lack of validity of the survey tool and the subjectivity of content elements'. The accompanying editorial describes the design as 'using Campbell's Urology as a gold standard'.
estimates.moderator_quote: The search engine Webcrawler® was used with the search term “prostate cancer” to generate a list of 75 websites which were reviewed for currency, disclosure, attribution, interactivity and content. A rating tool was designed including 50 elements considered essential for a comprehensive review of prostate cancer, and each website was judged for degree of coverage and accuracy (each rated on a scale of 1 to 3) of information for each element.
estimates.notes: The unit is an information element (a statement), not a website: the denominator is the 943 elements that the 39 sites actually covered, so elements a site simply omitted are not counted as errors (the authors note this separately as an 'error of omission' problem: 'high accuracy is tempered by poor balance, which may be considered equivalent to error of omission ... and can generate a misleading impression'). The 1% is rounded and the underlying count is not given; 1% of 943 is roughly 9 to 10 elements. Denominator is rank-truncated (top 75 of 390,770 hits, 16 of them dead links, 20 more without prostate cancer content), hence denom_selection curated. Data-collection date is never stated, so year is the publication year. Country coded Global: site nationality is never restricted or reported. Construct call: the paper is framed as a quality assessment, but accuracy was rated on its own 1-to-3 scale separate from coverage and against a textbook standard, which meets the INSTRUCTIONS §3 test for CONTENT; the coverage, currency, disclosure, attribution and balance components are QUALITY and were not extracted. QUOTE NOTE: the body of this text file interleaves the PDF's two print columns, so the Discussion copy of this sentence is not contiguous; the abstract copy, which is single-column and identical in numbers, is quoted instead (the Discussion writes 'covered in 39 sites' and puts the category labels in quotation marks).

missed_or_uncertain: Considered and not extracted: (1) '99% of information being "mostly" or "completely correct"' — the accurate complement of the row above, not a second estimate. (2) Coverage-depth distribution of the same 943 elements (25% mostly addressed, 34% more than minimally addressed, 40% minimally addressed) — completeness, a QUALITY dimension with no bearing on falsity; no row made, since the review excludes such rows from prevalence and the paper already yields a genuine accuracy share. (3) All other quality indicators, which are counts or means rather than falsity shares: 9 of 39 sites updated within 6 months, 24 of 39 with no update date, references complete on 5 sites and absent on 28, disclaimer on 18 of 39, contact mechanism on 38, level of evidence on 7 of 39, mean 24 elements covered per site (range 6 to 43), mean coverage rating 1.8 (range 1.0 to 2.6), mean total coverage score 45 of 150, balance-of-evidence counts (25 sites discussed screening but only 10 covered at least 2 of 4 elements adequately; imbalance in 13 of 33 sites), Table 2 disclosure counts, and the per-site accuracy means (rating 3 on 17 sites, 2.9 on 15, 2.8 on 5, 2.7 or 2.6 on one each; overall 2.9; 'only 6 sites had an accuracy rating of less than 2.9'). Site-level shares such as 6/39 would have to be computed and describe a quality-score threshold, not a falsity rate. (4) Element-specific error counts (Gleason sum defined completely on 27 sites, 20 completely correct and 7 mostly correct; PSA screening guidelines on 16 sites, 12 completely correct and 4 mostly correct) — these give no 'mostly incorrect' count, so no falsity share can be formed from them without computing complements. (5) 'Up to 45% of patients with prostate cancer are using the Internet for self-education' — cited from other papers, barred by R8. (6) Hellawell et al's mean website score of 50.7 — also cited from elsewhere.

rob.design: Cross-sectional structured review of websites. One search engine (Webcrawler), one unmodified query ('prostate cancer'), 390,770 hits, top 75 taken; 16 were dead links and 20 of the 59 live sites had no prostate cancer content, leaving 39 evaluated (6 academic or government, 11 nonprofit, 12 commercial, 4 physician or private health care, 4 personal or self-help, 2 news). A site needed at least 5 covered elements to enter. Instrument built from the 1997 'Criteria for Assessing the Quality of Health Information on the Internet' and Bertrand et al, with content elements taken from Campbell's Urology, 7th edition; five components rated (currency, disclosure, attribution, interactivity, content), content split into coverage and accuracy, each on a 1 to 3 scale. Rated by 'the research team'; the number of raters, their independence, any double coding and any reliability statistic are not reported. Data-collection date not reported. Authors flag the tool's lack of validity, the subjectivity of the elements, the single search engine and the small number of sites; the editorial comment questions whether a typical searcher would retrieve the same 39 sites.
